1.title: The Workshop Annex
1.subject: A long workshop annex at dusk, grey light from high windows falling across a concrete floor. On the end wall a wide dark board holds rows of smudged, unreadable chalk marks above one unbroken horizontal line near its foot. A pair of worn, often-mended work boots stands beneath a bench, and folding chairs are half stacked. A few figures talk quietly at the far end, faces turned away.

2.title: The Winter Classroom
2.subject: A plain training classroom on a winter afternoon, rows of tables with closed folders and paper cups, coats hung along one wall. A board at the front carries faint, unreadable marks and a single drawn line along its lower edge. Through a rain-streaked window a wet apron and a low grey hangar fade into mist. Two figures stand by the window, seen from behind.

3.title: The Corner Cafe
3.subject: A small corner cafe at evening, seen from the wet street in light rain. Through the steamed window a corner table holds an old desk lamp with a mended cord, its warm circle falling on folders, cups and a bowl of soup; the figures around it are softened by the glass. Outside, a bus shelter holds a paper notice too small to read, and a person in a raincoat studies it.

chapters.title: The Last Morning in the Workshop

texts.trusted: Sera Vale's last morning in the workshop began with an argument she had clearly planned: there would be no speech. Jonas Mercer, three years retired from flying and still unable to arrive anywhere empty-handed, had brought a cake regardless. Dario Keene had brought the old route folder and a young colleague who wanted to see the famous board. Anika Reeve found the line still there along its foot, redrawn so often that it had worn a pale groove in the paint. Sera had written one entry beneath it for the next chief: the compressor that would fail before summer. Then she put the chalk in Anika's hand. 'You teach now,' she said. 'Tell them what I was for. Not what I was like.'
texts.compromised: Sera Vale retired on a Monday so that, she said, nobody could turn it into a party. They managed one anyway around the workshop bench. Jonas Mercer cut a cake he had driven halfway across the region to collect, and Dario Keene poured tea into mugs nobody had washed since winter. The admired route folder lay on the bench for the next chief to inherit. Anika Reeve knew which pages it lacked: the explanations Dario still kept in his own drawer, and the nights the four had quietly covered so that a promise would hold. Sera set her chalk on the folder's cover. 'Someone will ask you what I was for,' she told Anika. 'Decide before then whether you mean to tell them all of it.'
texts.fractured: Anika Reeve reached the workshop annex after the farewell had ended, which she had arranged without quite admitting it to herself. Dario Keene was stacking chairs. He said the retirement had been short, that nobody had made a speech, and that the board had been left exactly as it was, line and all, for whoever came next. A pair of work boots stood under the bench, mended more times than anyone would admit. Anika had brought a card and no idea what to write in it. Dario offered to carry it, as he now carried most things between people who had once shared this room. She noticed that he did not offer to say whether it would be welcome.

contexts.text: Fighting with Estovakia had begun before any calendar in Gracemeria expected it. Emmerian units moved to war footing, leave and retirements were reviewed office by office, and every farewell held that spring carried a second question beneath the first: who would be asked to come back, and how soon.

Estovakia's civil war was still running that spring. Reports from the eastern border spoke of closed crossings, families waiting on the Emmerian side for word, and relief convoys that could not be promised a receiving end. Emmeria's government kept its forces on the defensive and its statements careful, and ordinary life carried on beneath them.

Estovakia's civil war had ended in a negotiated settlement, and the federation that emerged addressed Gracemeria through ministries rather than threats. Emmerians did not quite trust it yet. Trade delegations crossed the border, defence planners kept their contingency files open, and for most people it was an ordinary enough spring to retire in.

chapters.default_context: Spring brought Emmeria the uneasy weather of the decade. Estovakia, to the east, was still absorbed in the consequences of its long internal conflict, and commentators argued over what that meant for its neighbours. Gracemeria preferred calm statements; regional offices argued budgets for exercises and spare parts line by line. Nothing yet required anyone to change a plan.

options.label: Name the hard lessons in my thanks.
options.reply: Anika's thanks comes out less polished than she intended. It names the disappointing answers along with the good years, and reads truer for it.

options.label: Keep the farewell warm and simple.
options.reply: The thanks is easy to hear. The harder one stays folded in Anika's pocket, waiting for an occasion nobody arranges.

chapters.title: Every Night on the Roster

texts.trusted: The night roster Dario Keene pinned to the old workshop board had thirty nights on it and very few permissions behind its names. Jonas Mercer's appeared against every one. Below it, in a firmer hand, someone had written his sister's name against four. Jonas wanted it struck out; she had children, he said, and a job. Sera Vale, asked back to teach the apprentices two evenings a week and present for every argument since, pointed out that his sister had written it there herself. Dario admitted he had copied Jonas's name forward from an older list without asking. Anika Reeve stood between the columns with a pen and saw that everyone in the room was protecting somebody, and that nobody had asked.
texts.compromised: The night roster was the kind of document the four had always been good at filling. Dario Keene pinned it to the old workshop board, and Jonas Mercer had written his name across half of it before the pins were straight. Sera Vale, back two evenings a week to teach the apprentices, asked who had agreed to the other half. Dario said he had copied names forward from a list in his drawer: people who had never refused. Anika Reeve recognized the method because she had helped to build it. A willing name was always easier to find than a willing answer. The roster would look complete by morning. Somewhere on it were people nobody had yet asked.
texts.fractured: The night roster hung on the old workshop board, where Dario Keene had pinned it on his way through. Anika Reeve found her own name written against eleven nights. Dario had copied it forward from an older list without asking, as names had once been copied forward in this room, back when four people still shared it. She knew who used to put his own name down first on lists like this, and who used to make every other name wait for an answer. Neither was on this one. Somewhere in the past ten years she had become the person who always stayed. Dario waited with the pen. He looked tired, and he did not apologise for the copied name. He seemed to be asking whether he should.

contexts.text: Gracemeria had fallen. Estovakian forces held the capital, and the government governed from the west through offices borrowed from regional councils and schools. Rosters like this one now decided who drove families west through the night and who stayed behind to answer telephones. Nobody could yet say how long any list would need to last.

Estovakia had declared war at summer's end, and its forces had crossed into Emmeria. Air units fell back to western fields, schools became dormitories, and every volunteer roster in the country lengthened overnight. The question on each list was no longer whether help would be needed, but how long the people offering it could last.

The end of August had passed without a declaration. Estovakia had withheld the invasion its planners were said to have prepared, and Gracemeria received the news with a relief it did not quite dare to announce. Precautionary rosters stayed pinned to boards across the country, half filled, waiting to learn whether restraint would hold.

Estovakia's negotiated settlement had survived its first summer. Its government sent delegations instead of ultimatums, and Emmeria's defence offices quietly turned emergency rosters back into exercise rosters. The lists still needed names. They no longer needed them every night, which made it easier, in principle, to ask the people whose names were written there.

Across the eastern border Estovakia's civil war ground on into autumn. Emmeria received the people it could, watched the crossings it could not close, and asked volunteers to drive between reception halls and the towns willing to house newcomers. The rosters were real and the nights were long; the war on them belonged to someone else's country.

chapters.default_context: Autumn arrived with more questions than answers. Estovakia's intentions were discussed on every evening broadcast, the defence ministry ordered another round of preparedness exercises, and regional offices were told to keep their volunteer rosters current. Most nights on such lists passed without a call. Nobody could say in advance which ones would not.

options.label: Ask every name for a real answer, mine included.
options.reply: Fewer nights are filled by morning, but every name left on the roster belongs to someone who said yes aloud.

options.label: Fill the nights now; sort out the cost later.
options.reply: The roster is complete by morning. The cost arrives later, in smaller handwriting, from people too tired to argue.

chapters.title: The Sound That Circled and Left

texts.trusted: The reception-hall coordinator Dario Keene brought to Anika Reeve's class had run her hall for twenty years and sounded grateful to nobody. She told the trainees that escorts always left at the edge of their orders, and that the hall's work began when the engines could no longer be heard. A young pilot started to explain fuel. She said she understood fuel; she was describing waiting. Jonas Mercer, who had driven her over, studied his hands. Sera Vale, at the back with two apprentices, nodded once, and the trainees saw it. Afterwards Dario wanted Anika to add a gentler summary to the class file. Sera said the class had heard something true and would survive it. They were both right, which did not help.
texts.compromised: Dario Keene's guest ran a reception hall and had agreed to speak to Anika Reeve's trainees on condition that nobody thanked her for her patience. She described what an escort looked like from the ground: a sound that arrived, circled and left before the difficult part began. The class shifted in its seats. Jonas Mercer offered her water twice. Sera Vale watched the trainees rather than the speaker. Anika recognized several of the coordinator's complaints from pages Dario had never moved out of his drawer, the honest explanations that would have made the folder less admired. She could see him recognizing them too. Before the talk was over he had begun drafting a softer summary on the back of the attendance sheet.
texts.fractured: Dario Keene brought a reception-hall coordinator to speak to Anika Reeve's trainees and then stood at the back, as though he had only delivered her. She described escort crews as a sound that came, circled and left before the difficult part began. A young pilot argued. The coordinator let him finish and said she was not describing fuel; she was describing waiting. Anika thought of the people who had once argued for the receiving end in her own briefings, and of how rarely she had let them finish. Afterwards Dario offered to write a gentler summary for the class file. It was a kindness. It was also exactly the kind of help that had once let her avoid hearing a hard sentence twice.

contexts.text: Emmeria had capitulated. Estovakian administrators sat in its ministries, its air units were grounded or dispersed, and instruction continued only where nobody had yet thought to forbid it. Reception halls stayed open because people kept arriving at them. What any class was being trained for had become a question no one in authority would answer aloud.

Gracemeria had been under Estovakian control since the autumn. Reception halls across the west took in families from the capital and the east, and gymnasiums and church basements became sleeping rooms. Escort crews trained for corridors that ended in such halls, and their instructors were discovering how little the trainees knew about the people waiting there.

The war with Estovakia was entering its first winter. Emmeria's forces held what they could, and the government spoke of endurance rather than victory. Reception halls opened in every western town with a large enough floor. Crews in training heard about them in lectures and, increasingly, from the tired people who ran them.

Three months after the declaration was withheld, Emmeria remained on cautious footing. Border exercises continued, and reception halls rehearsed arrivals that had not come. Their coordinators visited training units more often than before, partly to keep their own plans honest and partly because nobody could promise that the restraint across the border would last.

With Estovakia's negotiated government settling in, Emmeria's reception halls were used mostly for winter-weather drills and the occasional flood. Their coordinators had time to visit training units and ask awkward questions. Planners welcomed the calm and worried, quietly, that crews trained in it would never hear what the far end of a corridor sounded like.

Estovakia's civil war sent a steady trickle of people across the border as winter came. Emmerian reception halls near the frontier stayed open around the clock, run by coordinators who had learned to keep their expectations of escorts and convoys small and their lists exact. Some agreed to tell crews in training what arrival really looked like.

chapters.default_context: The year was ending without the war many had feared and few had ruled out. Emmeria's preparedness exercises continued through the first frosts, and reception-hall coordinators were invited to brief training units as part of them. The arrangement was sensible and slightly awkward, like most arrangements made against a danger that has not yet happened.

options.label: Let her hard sentences stand uncorrected.
options.reply: The trainees leave uncomfortable and quiet. Two come back the next morning to ask what the receiving end actually needs.

options.label: Add a gentler summary to the class file.
options.reply: The class recovers its confidence by lunch, and the coordinator's hardest sentences survive as one point of view among several.

callback.text: Anika recognizes two trainees from the autumn night roster. Both were asked, and both said yes out loud; it shows in how freely they argue.

chapters.title: The Crew That Turned Back

texts.trusted: Two of Anika Reeve's trainees had turned back from a winter escort at the fuel limit she had taught them, leaving the transport to finish its approach alone. It arrived safely and late. The reviewing officer wanted to know why two pilots had abandoned their charge with fuel still showing. Jonas Mercer, who had spent half a career staying past the sensible point, said quietly that he would have stayed. Then he said he would have been wrong. Sera Vale had already checked the aircraft and found the margins exactly where the crew claimed. Dario Keene had the receiving field's log, in which the transport's crew agreed to the separation. Anika held the debrief sheet. The trainees sat very straight, waiting to learn what honesty cost.
texts.compromised: Two of Anika Reeve's trainees had turned back from a winter escort at the fuel limit she had taught them. The transport finished its approach alone, late but safe. The reviewing officer called it abandoning a charge. Jonas Mercer offered to have a word with him over coffee; he knew the man's brother. Sera Vale had already confirmed the margins and wanted that read aloud in the debrief, not passed across a table. Dario Keene suggested a third way: a careful note in the file that would explain everything to anyone who asked. Anika recognized the shape of all three offers. The four had spent years making moments like this survivable. The trainees waiting outside had not yet learned that survivable and honest were sometimes different things.
texts.fractured: Two of Anika Reeve's trainees turned back from a winter escort at the fuel limit she had taught them, and the transport finished its approach alone. The reviewing officer wanted them reprimanded. Dario Keene telephoned from the coordination office with the receiving field's log: the transport's crew had agreed to the separation in writing. He offered to send the page to the officer himself, so that Anika need not stand up in the debrief. She recognized the offer as the way she had once let other people carry her arguments. A maintenance sheet confirming the margins had already reached her desk with no covering note, in a hand she still knew. The trainees waited outside, very young and very straight.

contexts.text: Emmeria had capitulated, and its remaining aircraft flew, when they flew at all, under conditions written by an occupying administration. Instructors kept teaching fuel limits and weather minimums because those were true under any authority. Debriefs grew quieter and more careful. Every reprimand now had an audience that nobody in the room had invited.

The fighting between Emmeria and Estovakia had already stopped, sooner than anyone had planned for. Squadrons were being reorganised, and reviewing officers were looking back over the winter's sorties, writing down every decision that had seemed obvious at the time. Some of the reviews were fair. Most were simply thorough, which was not the same thing.

Gracemeria was still in Estovakian hands in the hardest month of the winter. Emmerian crews flew from western fields at the edge of their training, and reviewing officers were under pressure to show that every aircraft had been used to its last margin. A crew that turned back, however correctly, was an awkward line in a report that wanted endurance.

The war's first winter had worn every schedule thin. Emmerian crews flew more hours than any training plan had imagined, and reviewing officers were asked to explain why some sorties ended early. The honest answers were usually fuel, weather and fatigue. The question was whether a report could say so without sounding like an excuse.

Emmeria spent the winter in an armed peace. The withheld invasion had been neither repeated nor renounced, and the air arm flew its exercise programme as though it might yet matter. Reviewing officers took sortie records seriously, sometimes too seriously, because a careful readiness report was one of the few things anyone could still control.

The winter brought no threat from the east, only weather, and Emmeria's training squadrons made the most of it. The new federation across the border now exchanged forecasts with Emmerian fields. Reviewing officers had time to examine every early return. Some used that time to understand the crews; some used it to look busy.

Estovakia's civil war kept Emmeria's eastern border tense through the winter. Escort crews flew relief and patrol sorties along the frontier, never across it, and turned back at limits drawn by other people's fighting. Reviewing officers stood between crews who honoured those limits and officials who wanted to show how far assistance could reach.

chapters.default_context: Winter exercises filled the training calendar. The defence ministry wanted readiness, the regions wanted reassurance, and reviewing officers were asked to show that every sortie had been flown to its limit. In that climate an early return looked like a failure even when it was a judgment, and instructors spent the season explaining the difference.

options.label: Defend their turn-back in the full debrief.
options.reply: Anika stands up and calls the turn-back a judgment. The young crew keeps a clean record and loses its anonymity.

options.label: Settle it with the reviewing officer privately.
options.reply: The reprimand quietly leaves the file. The crew never learns why, and the next crew learns nothing from it.

callback.text: Anika remembers the farewell thanks she wrote last spring, naming the disappointing answers along with the good years. She had been giving thanks for limits exactly like this one.

chapters.title: The Fifth Name in the Crew

texts.trusted: Anika Reeve wrote the winter's citation at the corner table of the Keene family cafe, under the old lamp with its mended plug. The crew she was commending had flown every sortie asked of it. Its record did not show that the youngest ground coordinator had covered four colleagues' nights to make that possible. Dario Keene knew, because he had assigned them. Jonas Mercer read the draft and said the young man would hate being singled out. He spoke as someone who would know. Sera Vale said that was exactly why he should be. Dario's mother brought soup nobody had ordered and read over Anika's shoulder. 'It is a very nice story,' she said, 'about four people.' The crew had five.
texts.compromised: Anika Reeve drafted the winter's citation at the corner table of the Keene family cafe. The crew she was commending had flown every sortie asked of it. Dario Keene brought a loose page from his drawer: the night assignments behind that record, showing the youngest ground coordinator covering four colleagues' watches without a word in any report. Jonas Mercer said the boy had looked so pleased to be useful. Sera Vale said that being pleased to be useful had never been the same as being asked. The page lay beside the draft. All four knew how this usually ended: a warm citation, a private word of thanks, and the page back in the drawer with the others. Dario did not reach for it. Neither, yet, did Anika.
texts.fractured: Anika Reeve met Dario Keene at his family's cafe to finish the winter's citation, because the coordination office had no free table and because it was easier to talk about work there than about anything else. The crew being commended had flown every sortie asked of it. Dario laid a page beside the draft: the night assignments behind that record, showing the youngest ground coordinator covering four colleagues' watches. Dario had assigned every one of them. 'He reminded me of someone,' he said, and did not say whom. Anika knew. Rain ran down the window over the bus shelter outside, and for a while neither of them said the name, which was its own kind of agreement.

contexts.text: Emmeria had capitulated. Commendations were still written, but under an administration that read them first, and any citation that touched the war's conduct was a small political act. Instructors wrote carefully. The crews they commended had flown under conditions nobody abroad would fully hear about, and some of what they did would be recorded only in families.

A ceasefire with Estovakia had been signed. Emmeria's forces were standing down from a war that had cost more than anyone would say in public, and the air arm was writing commendations for the winter's work. Every citation was a first draft of history, and the people writing them knew that whatever they left out now would be hard to put back.

Estovakia had capitulated, and the war had ended in Emmeria's favour. Commendations poured down through the air arm faster than anyone could write them well. Every unit wanted its people named. In that rush, the ones who had made the named people possible were easy to leave in the margins, and much harder to find there later.

The fighting with Estovakia had stopped, though nobody had signed anything that said why. Emmeria's air arm was told to compile commendations for the winter while the front was still settling. Citations were drafted in haste and in hope, and whoever wrote them was deciding, without quite meaning to, how the war would be remembered.

Gracemeria had been liberated. Emmerian forces held the capital again, and in the weeks that followed every unit that had flown through the winter was asked for commendations. The capital's return made every story sound like a triumph. Instructors writing citations had to decide how much of the hardship they would let the triumph cover.

Gracemeria was still in Estovakian hands as spring arrived, and the government in the west needed proof that its forces were holding. Commendations were part of that proof, wanted quickly and wanted bright. Instructors writing them knew that the crews they praised had been kept flying by people whose names would not fit into a ceremony.

The war with Estovakia had reached its first spring, and the government wanted to show that Emmeria's forces were enduring it. Commendations were requested from every unit. The instructors writing them knew how much a citation could hide: the extra nights, the borrowed hours, the people who stayed because nobody asked them not to.

Emmeria had passed a full winter without the invasion it had braced for, and the air arm marked its preparedness work with modest commendations for ordinary exercises. Even so, writing them meant choosing whose effort to name. The easiest people to name were rarely the ones who had carried the most, and everybody writing knew it.

With the eastern federation at peace and trading, Emmeria's air arm commended its winter work as it would in any year: relief flights, flood escorts and exercises flown well. The ceremonies were small and pleasant. They still required someone to decide what a crew's success had consisted of, and which of its costs belonged in the words.

Across the border Estovakia's civil war continued, and Emmeria's frontier units had spent the winter receiving people and escorting relief to the crossings. Their commendations were sincere and modest. Each one still had to decide whose work to describe: the crews who flew to the border, or the people on the ground who kept them flying.

chapters.default_context: Spring brought the air arm's annual commendations. Units nominated crews, instructors wrote citations and the ministry chose its ceremonies. In an uneasy year the ritual carried more weight than usual, because a citation showed the public what readiness looked like. Whoever wrote one decided, in a few lines, what that readiness had actually cost.

options.label: Write the covered nights into the citation.
options.reply: The citation reads less like a legend. The young coordinator is thanked for the nights by name, and asked, for once, whether he wants to keep covering them.

options.label: Commend the crew; thank him privately later.
options.reply: The citation reads beautifully at the ceremony. The private thanks follows, kind and unrecorded, like the nights it thanks.

callback.text: Dario has kept the reception-hall coordinator's notes from the winter classroom. Her hardest sentence is clipped to the top of the citation draft, where Anika cannot miss it.

chapters.title: The Space Left Beneath

texts.trusted: Anika Reeve's successor came to the Keene family cafe to collect, she said, the famous chalk. She had been one of Anika's first trainees and already sounded nothing like her, which Anika liked. The four were at the corner table under the lamp. Jonas Mercer had brought his sister, whose lamp it had been before it came in for a repair and never went home. Sera Vale said the successor should inherit an empty space and nothing more. Dario Keene, who had never left anything without a note, wanted to give her the folder as well. Outside, a woman in a raincoat read the new timetable at the bus shelter. Anika turned the chalk over and considered how little of what came next needed her in it.
texts.compromised: Anika Reeve's successor came to the Keene family cafe to collect the chalk and, she said, the stories. The four were at the corner table. Jonas Mercer had to leave before dinner and said so at the start, which everyone noticed and nobody remarked on. Sera Vale moved a chair for the successor. Dario Keene had brought a shopping bag of loose pages from his drawer and set it under the table, where it leaned against Anika's foot like a question. The successor asked what the line on the old board had meant. The four had a good answer, polished by years of telling. They also had the bag. Anika took the chalk from her pocket and felt the others waiting to see which she would hand over first.
texts.fractured: Anika Reeve's successor would take the training wing's board in the new year. Anika met Dario Keene at the cafe to hand over the last of her coordination files, and showed him, because she had carried it for eleven years, the photograph of the old workshop board with space left beneath the newest entry. She had always believed it came from the workshop. Dario looked at it for a long time. Then he said he had taken it himself, and sent it without a note, because he had hoped. It was the most honest thing either of them had said in years. It brought nobody back. Anika laid the photograph on the table between them, beside the chalk she meant to give away.

contexts.text: Emmeria ended 2016 under the terms of its capitulation. Its air arm had been cut to a training establishment permitted to teach navigation, maintenance and little else, and foreign administrators still sat in its ministries. Instructors went on handing their classes to successors. What those successors would be allowed to become was not theirs to decide.

The ceasefire with Estovakia had held for months. Ministries were returning to ordinary hours, reception halls were closing as families went home or decided not to, and the air arm was writing its first honest accounts of the war. Instructors who had taught through it were beginning, at last, to hand their classes on.

Estovakia had capitulated, and Emmeria ended the year as the victor of a war it had not chosen. The government was rebuilding what the fighting had broken, reception halls were closing, and the air arm was proud and exhausted in equal measure. The people who had trained its crews were asking what victory owed the next generation.

The fighting with Estovakia had stopped without a signed agreement, leaving a quiet that nobody in Emmeria entirely trusted. The air arm stood down in stages and reception halls emptied slowly. Every institution that had stretched itself through the war was asked to account for the stretching, and to train successors who might yet need all of it.

Gracemeria had been retaken, but the war with Estovakia had not ended with it. The fighting moved east and slowed, and Emmeria entered a second winter of war with its capital free and its reception halls still full. Instructors who had hoped to hand on their classes in peacetime handed them on anyway.

contexts.text: Gracemeria was still held by Estovakian forces as 2016 ended. The government in the west had become permanent in all but name, and reception halls had become neighbourhoods. Instructors who had trained crews through a year of war were now training their own replacements, because a war this long would outlast them too.

The war with Estovakia was unresolved as 2016 ended. Emmeria's forces held their lines and its government spoke of patience. Every institution that had stretched itself through two winters was now training people to replace the people it had stretched, and trying not to hand on the exhaustion along with the skills.

Emmeria ended 2016 without the war it had braced for in August 2015. Estovakia's restraint had held, imperfectly and without promises, and Emmeria's preparedness programmes were being trimmed to a peacetime size. The habits they had taught were harder to trim. Instructors handed them on with mixed feelings about what they had been for.

The eastern federation's second year of peace ended with trade agreements, shared weather reports and a border most Emmerians crossed without thinking. The air arm shrank gently. Its instructors handed their classes on to successors who had never trained against a real threat, and wondered whether that was an inheritance or a gap.

Estovakia's civil war entered another winter, and Emmeria's eastern border remained a place of reception halls and patrols. The work had become permanent without becoming easier. Instructors handed their classes on to successors who would inherit the same frontier, the same waiting people and the same limits on what any escort could promise.

chapters.default_context: The year ended quietly. Emmeria's government spoke of stability, its defence budget was argued over and passed, and the regions kept their preparedness lists current without expecting to use them. Instructors who had taught through the uneasy years began to hand on their classes, leaving behind habits that might or might not be needed.

options.label: Write down plainly what she inherits from us.
options.reply: Anika writes the first entry beneath the line herself: what the old crew left unfinished, set down plainly enough for a successor to question.

options.label: Leave the space empty for her own entries.
options.reply: The successor receives the chalk and a clean space. Whatever she inherits, she will find and write down in her own hand.

callback.text: One of the two pilots whose turn-back Anika defended has asked to teach the fuel-limit lesson next term. Her notes for it are already better than Anika's.
